analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers erase student loan debt in bankruptcy once the loan has been due for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, student loans are almost never wiped out because borrowers must prove 'undue hardship,' a very high bar. This bill would have let a borrower discharge a student loan through bankruptcy without proving hardship, as long as the loan had first come due more than five years earlier. It was introduced in July 2018, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers who remain in financial distress years after their loans came due would gain a realistic path to a fresh start through bankruptcy, instead of facing a hardship standard that almost no one meets.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the bankruptcy code so a student loan can be discharged without proving undue hardship if the loan first became due more than five years before the bankruptcy filing.
Removes the main barrier that keeps student loans, unlike nearly all other consumer debt, from being canceled in bankruptcy.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders and servicers would absorb more losses when loans are discharged, and for federal student loans, the cost of forgiven balances would fall on taxpayers. Lenders might also charge higher rates to offset the added risk.

drawbacks.text: The bill would not have helped people already holding loans: under the bill's terms, it applies only to educational loans received after the law's effective date, which was set at one year after enactment.
Even for covered loans, a borrower would have to wait more than five years after the loan first came due before discharging it, so relief would be slow even in the best case.
Making student debt easier to discharge shifts losses onto lenders and, for federal loans, onto taxpayers, and could lead lenders to charge more or lend less.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but narrow: it would not touch loans people already had, and it would still require a five-year wait before bankruptcy could wipe out a covered loan. For borrowers caught in that window, it offers little; for future borrowers in long-term distress, it restores a bankruptcy protection that applies to most other kinds of debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lou Correa introduced the bill on July 26, 2018.
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill never advanced past the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders and servicers, and the federal loan portfolio, are better off because the bill died: debt they hold stayed much harder to discharge in bankruptcy, and no added discharge losses were imposed on them.

for.name: Rep. Lou Correa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor when it was introduced.

for.name: 1 House Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no other support in the chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 26, 2018 and never reported the bill, held no hearing or markup, and never sent it to the floor.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 115th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the bill's single cosponsor were Democrats, no Republican backed it, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would let borrowers cancel loans in bankruptcy after five years due, turning nearly untouchable student debt into ordinary dischargeable debt. That directly cuts the value of loans these companies hold and service, which is why keeping the undue-hardship barrier matters to them.

Federal student loans fall under the same bankruptcy exception the bill amends, so more discharges would mean more forgiven balances borne by the Treasury. Borrowers seeking relief and the government collecting the debt are on opposite sides of the same dollar.
